entries.clue: Suit as may be worn by wealthy (8)

definitions.text: as may be worn by wealthy

blocks.note: one of the four suits in a pack of cards

blocks.clueFragment: as may be worn by wealthy
blocks.note: expensive jewels worn by the rich

annotation.surface: A remark about what sort of clothes rich people wear.
annotation.walkthrough: "Suit" looks like tailoring, which fits the talk of the wealthy wearing things; it is really the card suit.
annotation.definitionFit: Diamonds are one of the four suits in a deck of cards.

entries.clue: Paint picture of Claude’s crib, expertly ignoring parts (8)

indicators.note: we ignore the outer parts of the phrase and keep the letters running inside it

blocks.note: ClauDE’S CRIB, Expertly

annotation.surface: Someone paints a picture of the house where the painter Claude lived, doing it skilfully.
annotation.walkthrough: "Paint" and "Claude" suggest Monet, but painting a picture here is only figurative: to describe something in words.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: painting a picture of a scene in words means giving a vivid account of it.

entries.clue: Live-in childminder saving skin … her name? (3)

indicators.note: the skin is the outer layer, the first and last letters, which are saved, that is kept out of the answer

blocks.note: a nanny often lives with the family she works for
NANNY without its first and last letters

annotation.surface: Someone wonders what the name of the family’s live-in nanny is.
annotation.walkthrough: "Saving" here means except, as in "all saving one", so the nanny loses her skin. The question mark admits that Ann is just one example of a woman’s name.
annotation.definitionFit: Ann is a woman’s first name, so it could be her name.

entries.clue: Rock, passé, cut … (7)

blocks.note: out of fashion
to crop is to cut short

annotation.surface: A snippy verdict that rock music is old hat, trailing off into the next clue.
annotation.walkthrough: "Rock" reads as the music, which suits "passé"; it is actual stone. The dots join this clue to 4 down, whose surface continues the thought.
annotation.definitionFit: An outcrop is a piece of rock showing above the ground.

entries.clue: … record by Queen censored having fallen from favour (11)

blocks.note: a vinyl record is a disc
R = Regina, Latin for queen
cut before publication

annotation.surface: Carrying on from 3 down: a record by the band Queen was cut by the censors after they went out of fashion.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface pictures the rock band Queen, but the word only supplies R, the Latin Regina.
annotation.definitionFit: Something discredited has lost people’s trust or favour.

entries.clue: Walk – gosh – flipping healthy (4,2)

indicators.note: to flip something is to turn it over, so the letters run the other way

blocks.note: an exclamation of surprise, like gosh; flipped to HOO
fit = in good health

annotation.surface: Someone exclaims that walking is really, really good for you, with "flipping" as a mild swear word.
annotation.walkthrough: "Flipping" reads as a mild British intensifier, as in flipping healthy; it is really the instruction to turn OOH round.
annotation.definitionFit: To hoof it is an informal way of saying to walk somewhere.

entries.clue: Not fashionable, friendless originally: is Everyman folding? (7)

indicators.note: not having IN: the letters IN are taken out
friendless: the word without ALLY, a friend

blocks.note: the word itself, from which letters are removed
IN = fashionable, removed
ALLY = friend, removed as well
the setter says "is Everyman" as AM I

annotation.surface: An odd musing on whether the setter, lonely and out of fashion, is about to give up.
annotation.walkthrough: "Originally" looks like an instruction to take first letters, but it is the word to be cut down. "Folding" pretends to mean giving up; it is the paper craft.
annotation.definitionFit: Origami is the Japanese art of folding paper into shapes.

entries.clue: Evidence of shark; men doing badly in fishy film (7,4)

indicators.note: the letters are put together badly, into a new order

blocks.note: a fin above the water shows a shark is there
the letters of MEN DOING rearranged

annotation.surface: A review of a shark film, where the actors are no good.
annotation.walkthrough: "Doing badly" reads as the actors failing; "doing" is also the fodder, so only "badly" is really the signal.
annotation.definitionFit: Finding Nemo is the Pixar animated film about a clownfish, so a fishy film.

entries.clue: A little faint, wan gynaecologist with nasal tone (6)

indicators.note: only a little of the phrase is used: a run of letters inside it

blocks.note: fainT, WAN GYnaecologist

annotation.surface: A description of a doctor who looks pale and weak and talks through the nose.
annotation.walkthrough: The run of adjectives about the doctor hides the answer across three words.
annotation.definitionFit: A twangy voice has a sharp, nasal sound.

entries.clue: That’s a nit I see – just a bit – get clean! (8)

definitions.note: "get clean" means make clean, a verb like SANITISE

indicators.note: just a bit of the phrase is used, a run of letters inside it

blocks.note: That’S A NIT I SEe

annotation.surface: Someone spots a head louse egg and demands a scrub.
annotation.walkthrough: The nit in the surface is exactly why you would sanitise, which helps the disguise.
annotation.definitionFit: To sanitise something is to make it clean and free of germs.

entries.clue: Where a waltz started in ‘80s pop hit (6)

blocks.note: the Viennese waltz grew up in the Austrian capital
Ultravox’s 1981 hit single

annotation.surface: A trivia question about a waltz that began inside a pop song of the 1980s.
annotation.walkthrough: "Vienna" by Ultravox reached number 2 in the UK charts in 1981.
annotation.definitionFit: The waltz became popular in Vienna, and Vienna was also the title of a well-known 1980s song.

entries.clue: It spins forward – and backward? (5)

indicators.note: the word reads the same in both directions

blocks.note: a five-letter word spelt identically in both directions

annotation.surface: A riddle about something that turns one way and then the other.
annotation.walkthrough: "Forward and backward" seems to describe the spinning, as if it changed direction; it describes the spelling.
annotation.definitionFit: A rotor is the part of a machine, such as a helicopter, that spins.

entries.clue: Flatus scent – moved: discretion (11)

indicators.note: the letters are moved around into a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 11 letters

annotation.surface: Someone passes wind and moves away from the smell, which is the polite thing to do.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a joke: discretion is exactly what the moment calls for. Flatus is the medical word for wind from the bowel.
annotation.definitionFit: Tactfulness is care not to embarrass or offend, which is discretion.

entries.clue: Studying again, finally, Oscar Wilde: where was his Gaol? (9)

indicators.note: take the final letter of each of the next words

blocks.note: last letters of OscaR WildE
Wilde wrote The Ballad of Reading Gaol

annotation.surface: Going back over Wilde’s work and wondering where his prison was.
annotation.walkthrough: Reading is an English town whose jail held Wilde, and he wrote a poem about it; the town name is spelt like the everyday word, which is how it slots in.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: going back over a text you have already read is studying it once more.

entries.clue: After components switched, Wills’s missus’s posh car is fun way to get about (6,5)

indicators.note: the parts of KATE’S ROLLER swap places, the car going first

blocks.note: a Roller is slang for a Rolls-Royce
the possessive S of missus’s, kept between the two parts
Prince William’s wife is Kate

annotation.surface: A gossip item about the Princess of Wales’s car being a fun ride.
annotation.walkthrough: Wills is the British nickname for Prince William, whose wife is Catherine, known as Kate. Read as KATE’S ROLLER, then swap the two parts round.
annotation.definitionFit: A roller skate is a boot on wheels, a fun way to move around.

entries.clue: Climbing down, band pick legal high (4-9)

indicators.note: intoxicated, so the letters are scrambled

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 13 letters

annotation.surface: A group of musicians choosing a legal high and then retreating from the choice.
annotation.walkthrough: "Legal high" reads as one phrase, a drug that is not banned; it has to be split, with "legal" as fodder and "high" as the signal.
annotation.definitionFit: Climbing down means retreating from a position, as does back-pedalling.

entries.clue: Public schoolboy sheltering second old Soviet (8)

indicators.note: the first part shelters, or holds, the second inside it

blocks.note: a pupil at Eton College
s = second

annotation.surface: A boy at a British private school giving shelter to an elderly Russian.
annotation.walkthrough: Eton is a famous British public school, which in Britain means a fee-paying private one. Estonia was part of the Soviet Union until 1991, so an Estonian could be an old Soviet citizen.
annotation.definitionFit: Estonia was once a Soviet republic, so an Estonian is a former Soviet.

entries.clue: Top politicians, decadent French-born set (5-8)

indicators.note: morally loose, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 13 letters

annotation.surface: A sneer at leading politicians as a decadent crowd born in France.
annotation.walkthrough: In the UK Parliament ministers and their opposite numbers sit on the front benches, so front-benchers are the senior figures.
annotation.definitionFit: Front-benchers are the senior MPs of the government and opposition.

entries.clue: With ceremony, keep watch (7)

blocks.note: to keep a festival or custom with due ritual, as one keeps the Sabbath
to look at carefully

annotation.surface: An instruction to stand guard in a formal way.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a guard told to keep watch formally; the first definition is actually keeping a ritual, as in observing the Sabbath.
annotation.definitionFit: You observe a holiday by keeping it, and you observe something by watching it.

entries.clue: Naval officer, a little indolent, put in ill-considered catnap (7)

indicators.note: just a little of the word: its first letter
that letter is put inside the rest
badly thought out, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: CATNAP rearranged
first letter of Indolent, placed inside CAPTA…N

annotation.surface: A lazy naval officer caught having an unwise nap on duty.
annotation.walkthrough: A snoozing officer makes a neat picture, and the nap itself supplies the letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym by rank: in the navy it is the officer commanding a ship, above a commander.

entries.clue: Time to go with the Blues? (6)

blocks.note: musical time: the beat
the word that pairs with blues in the name of a musical style, R&B

annotation.surface: A gloomy thought that it is time to give in to sadness.
annotation.walkthrough: "Time to go" reads as a phrase about leaving; it splits after "Time". The question mark marks the second part as a hint rather than a synonym.
annotation.definitionFit: In music, time and rhythm both mean the beat, and rhythm is paired with blues in rhythm and blues.

entries.clue: Where lands steepen, in shelters, the writer’s going to sleep (at first) (9)

indicators.note: the next part goes in the shelters
take the first letter of sleep

blocks.note: hides are shelters, e.g. for birdwatchers
I’LL = I will, the writer speaking
first letter of Sleep

annotation.surface: The setter is going to find a shelter on steep ground and nod off.
annotation.walkthrough: "The writer" is the setter speaking of themself as I. The comma after "shelters" makes it look like a list, but the next two pieces both go inside.
annotation.definitionFit: Hillsides are the slopes of hills, where the land rises steeply.

entries.clue: In favour of second ad (5)

blocks.note: pro = for, in favour of
mo = a moment, a second

annotation.surface: Someone backing a second advertisement.
annotation.walkthrough: "Second" is a noun here, a short time, not the adjective it seems to be.
annotation.definitionFit: A promo is a short promotional advertisement.

entries.clue: That man is smothered by right-wing presumption (6)

indicators.note: the first part is smothered, wrapped round, by the second

blocks.note: a Tory is a British Conservative
he = that man

annotation.surface: A complaint that some man is being crushed by conservative arrogance.
annotation.walkthrough: "Presumption" suggests arrogance in the surface; the definition uses its other sense, a supposition.
annotation.definitionFit: A theory is a supposition or presumption about how things are.

entries.clue: Getting to Italy, M. le Président will eat a kind of pasta (8)

indicators.note: the president eats, so takes inside, the letter A
the result reaches, is joined to, Italy’s I

blocks.note: Emmanuel Macron, President of France
the letter itself, eaten by MACRON
I is the international code for Italy

annotation.surface: The French president arrives in Italy and is going to eat some pasta.
annotation.walkthrough: The French wording points to a Frenchman, and the answer really is Italian food, so the picture holds together.
annotation.definitionFit: Macaroni is a type of pasta in short tubes.

entries.clue: Peculiar to regularly ignore ‘Howdy-do?’ (3)

indicators.note: skip every other letter, starting with the first

blocks.note: the 2nd, 4th and 6th letters of HOWDYDO

annotation.surface: Someone finds it strange to snub a friendly greeting.
annotation.walkthrough: Starting from the first letter, H, W, Y and O are ignored, leaving the letters in between; the hyphen does not count.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: something peculiar is out of the ordinary, strange.

entries.clue: Primarily, man espousing strange ‘magnetism’ – especially restoratively? (6)

indicators.note: take the prime, first, letter of each word

blocks.note: Man Espousing Strange Magnetism Especially Restoratively

annotation.surface: A description of a man who believed in a strange kind of healing magnetism.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue both spells and describes its answer: Franz Mesmer, the 18th-century doctor who claimed to heal with animal magnetism, which gave us the word mesmerise.
annotation.definitionFit: Mesmer promoted animal magnetism as a healing force, so he was a man espousing strange magnetism for restoring health.

entries.clue: Bridled, noise of downpour heard (6,2)

indicators.note: what is heard is a sound, so spell a word that sounds the same

blocks.note: the sound of rain falling hard, said as a past-tense phrase

annotation.surface: Someone who bristled at the sound of heavy rain.
annotation.walkthrough: "Bridled" reads as taking offence, which suits the noise; the definition is the horse-riding sense, controlled with a bridle.
annotation.definitionFit: A horse bridled is reined in, held back by the reins.
